ADJ-09.title: An invariance screen for a bridging assumption, scored as a classifier
ADJ-09.question: Does instability across observed trials predict failure of a bridge used in a gap with no data, and does a screen on marginal effects fire under a valid bridge through non-collapsibility?
ADJ-09.design: K trials with differing covariate laws and a gap environment; Cochran's Q screen with abstention on marginal, conditional and standardized log odds ratios; valid bridge, drift visible in the trials, and drift confined to the gap; 20 cells and 3 controls, 1000 replicates each.

ADJ-15.title: Target moments released under differential privacy
ADJ-15.question: When a target trial releases covariate moments under differential privacy, how much does ignoring the added noise cost MAIC coverage at realistic arm sizes and budgets, does propagating its known variance repair it, and when do extra released moments stop paying for their share of the budget?
ADJ-15.answer: Privacy noise is not negligible at usable budgets for trial-sized targets: at epsilon 1 and 150 patients it was 8% to 60% of the estimate's variance and ignoring it cut coverage to 0.88 to 0.94; at 40 patients to 0.73. Its variance is known exactly, and adding it restored coverage in every scenario, conservatively where noise dominated. Releasing second moments pays only at larger budgets; at small ones it made MAIC infeasible in up to 87% of replicates.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: coverage ignoring the noise was as low as 0.883 at epsilon of at least 1 and targets of at least 150.

Propagating the known noise variance gave coverage of at least 0.926 in every private scenario, the minimum matching the non-private analysis's own misspecification; it reached 1.000 where noise dominated.
Releasing means and second moments with a split budget left no feasible weights in 45% to 87% of replicates at 40 to 150 patients and epsilon 0.5 to 1.
Under quadratic modification at epsilon 4 and 150 patients second moments cut RMSE from 0.229 to 0.171.
ADJ-15.not_answered: Laplace mechanism only; Gaussian mechanism, released correlations and overlap not varied. Results are conditional on feasible weights. Budget choice and governance are outside the study. Peer review has not been done.
ADJ-15.design: MAIC to Laplace-privatized target means or means and second moments, 48 cells crossing target size (40 to 500), privacy budget, released statistics and linear or quadratic effect modification; non-private, noise-ignored and noise-propagated analyses. 1000 replicates per cell.
ADJ-15.estimand: Target-population mean difference, A versus C, at the target trial's own covariate moments
methods_compared: MAIC to private moments, noise ignored
MAIC to private moments, noise variance propagated

CMP-12.title: Splitting a multi-arm trial's adjusted contrasts is conservative for one contrast and anticonservative for another
CMP-12.question: When a three-arm trial's population-adjusted contrasts share an arm and a weight vector, what is lost by treating them as independent, is the error ever anticonservative, and is dropping the trial cheaper?
CMP-12.answer: Ignoring the within-trial covariance errs in a direction set by the contrast, not by how the arms' effect modification aligns. The trial's own B-versus-C interval became conservative in every scenario, while the network A-versus-B interval, which borrows through the trial, fell below nominal in 15 of 30 scenarios. The shared-weighting part of the covariance took both signs but never reversed a contrast's error. Dropping the trial widened the network interval by 29% to 91%.
findings: Split, trial-alone d_BC: coverage 0.957 to 1.000, above nominal beyond 3 MCSE in 29 of 30 scenarios and below in none; DESIGN.md's alignment-sign prediction is withdrawn by its registered test.
Split, network d_AB: coverage 0.4 to 3.7 points below the stacked sandwich, below nominal beyond 3 MCSE in 15 of 30 scenarios against 0 for the stacked sandwich.
The shared-weighting covariance term was -22% to +15% of the Monte Carlo covariance, dominated by the shared-arm term.
Joint sandwiches recovered 0.76 to 1.15 (stacked) and 0.73 to 1.12 (weights fixed) of the Monte Carlo covariance; stacked trial-alone intervals covered 0.919 to 0.960.
Dropping the trial was unbiased and widened the network d_AB interval by a median 53%.
CMP-12.not_answered: Continuous outcome, linear modification, one three-arm trial in a fixed two-trial aggregate network; four-arm trials, the one-stage ML-NMR comparator and a bootstrap are not run, and target moments are fixed. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-12.design: Three-arm individual-data trial weighted by MAIC to a target, plus aggregate A-versus-C and B-versus-C trials in the target; 30 scenarios crossing effect-modification strength, its alignment across arms, target shift and shared-arm size; split, weights-fixed, stacked and drop analyses, network by generalized least squares.
CMP-12.estimand: d_AB, d_AC and d_BC in the target population

CMP-13.title: Separating within-trial from across-trial component effect modification
CMP-13.question: Component ML-NMR fits one shared interaction on a globally centered covariate, which algebraically forces the causal within-trial interaction to equal the confounded across-trial association. How much does that cost, when, and is the damage really caused by aggregate data as the catalog claims?
CMP-13.answer: Fitting one shared interaction matrix on a globally centered covariate is not pooling: for a binary modifier with study prevalence p_s it is algebraically identical to imposing that the causal within-trial coefficient equals the confounded across-trial one. In the model simulated, coverage of a nominal 95% interval for the causal interaction falls from 93.8% when that happens to be true to 17.2% when the two are equal and opposite, and further in networks whose contrasts move two components at once. Separating them costs about 5% in interval width and removes an order of magnitude of bias. The catalog's stated cause is incomplete: the loss is present with all twelve trials supplying individual data, so aggregate data are not necessary for it, but removing individual data roughly doubles the bias, so they amplify it.
findings: Coverage under the shared restriction degrades monotonically with the discordance between the within-trial and across-trial coefficients, from 93.8% at no discordance to 17.2% when they are equal and opposite, and it is worse in bundled component networks whose contrasts move two components at once than where every contrast isolates one.
Both separated estimators are nominal at every discordance examined, 92.6% to 96.3%, including under a nonlinear across-trial pattern where the linear split model is itself misspecified.

CMP-13 says aggregate studies cause the pull. With all twelve trials supplying individual patient data the shared model still has median absolute standardized bias 0.15 and coverage as low as 44.6%, so aggregate data are not necessary. But bias rises to 0.29 and coverage falls to 17.2% as individual data are removed, so they amplify it. The registered refutation threshold was narrowly missed (47% of cells against 50%) and we report that rather than moving it.

Where a component appears in no individual-data arm, the three methods behave in three different ways: the IPD-anchored estimator declines to report it in 100% of replicates; the shared model returns a confident -0.34 against a truth of zero, sourced entirely from the across-trial gradient; and the joint split returns intervals so wide that coverage approaches one, when it returns one at all.

A study-clustered sandwich, included so the comparison could not be won on the variance estimator, covered 75.4% to 92.4% where the shared model is correctly specified. With twelve clusters it is badly anticonservative, and it is reported as a finding rather than used as the comparator.
CMP-13.not_answered: The registered global analysis is uninformative and the regime split that produced a usable answer was prompted by observing that failure, so it is not prespecified. The general headline about component ML-NMR is not established: the likelihood and nuisance structures are not mapped onto the fixed- and random-effect specifications the implemented method offers, and free study-by-treatment effects or priors can absorb or alter the term the identity isolates. A maximum-likelihood analogue of component ML-NMR. Implemented ML-NMR is Bayesian and priors matter most where interactions are weakly identified, so the coverage numbers do not transfer to multinma; the algebra does, and therefore so does the direction. One binary modifier, a log link, a Poisson outcome, additive components with no synergy, no random treatment-effect heterogeneity, no inconsistency, and exactly reported study prevalences. Under the discordance patterns the split model is correctly specified, so the study measures the cost of an algebraically known restriction rather than establishing that real networks contain within/across disagreement or how large it typically is. Continuous or multiple correlated modifiers, misspecified aggregate covariate distributions, and time-to-event outcomes are untested. It does not touch IDN-05.
CMP-13.design: Twelve-trial two-component Poisson network with a binary effect modifier whose prevalence varies across studies, aggregate arms generated by exact integration. 320 scenarios crossing network structure, the discordance between within-trial and across-trial modification, IPD availability including a case where one component has no within-trial data at all, arm size and prevalence spread. 2000 replicates each.
CMP-13.estimand: Within-trial component interaction on the conditional log-rate scale

CMP-14.title: Prior-to-posterior contraction and effective likelihood rank measure information, not bias
CMP-14.question: CMP-14 asks for two default summaries, prior-to-posterior contraction per interaction and an effective likelihood rank, so an analyst sees when an aggregate-only interaction is held up by its prior. Would those summaries tell the analyst whether the reported interval covers?
CMP-14.answer: Not reliably, and the reason is structural. On an exact identity-link arm of 504 scenarios and a logit arm of 72, no threshold on contraction, on either effective-rank reading, or on the estimability screen separates scenarios whose 95% interval covers nominally from those that fail. The summaries are functions of Fisher information and the prior, so within one design they are exactly constant while coverage ranges from 0 to 0.96. They partly catch the failure they were designed for: contraction flags 59% of failures caused by a tight prior. They catch none of the 142 failures caused by a biased route, where the ecological route carries between-study confounding or the additivity route a synergy, because confounding moves the posterior mean and not its information. A clean contraction says the likelihood spoke, not that it was right. Every result is exploratory.
findings: All four registered statistics (contraction, target-level likelihood ratio, whole-model effective rank, estimability screen) take values shared by failing and nominal scenarios on both arms, so no threshold on any of them separates the classes. On E1 there are 251 failing and 169 nominal scenarios; on E2, 41 and 12.

On the identity link with known residual variance the posterior covariance does not involve the outcomes. Within one information state, spread, network size and prior, contraction, target ratio and effective rank are exactly constant across discordance and synergy levels while coverage ranges over 0.956.

Decomposed by cause (post hoc), 109 E1 failures come from a prior of SD 0.1 pulling a true interaction of 0.4 toward zero and 142 from a biased route. Contraction flags 58.7% of the first and 0% of the second; target ratio 41.3% and 0%; effective rank 56.0% and 0%.
Scenario pairs matched on spread, size and prior whose contraction differs by less than 0.02 differ in coverage by up to 0.951 on E1.

On the logit arm the rules score far better on average (contraction Youden 0.805 against 0.220 on E1) because 34 of its 41 failures sit at the tight prior and it has only 12 nominal scenarios. The overlap persists.

Three aggregate routes identify an interaction on the logit link, through differences in covariate means, covariate variances or baseline risk; only the first works on the identity link. None is randomized.
CMP-14.not_answered: Nothing here is confirmatory: E1 was computed before its protocol existed, E2's separation rules were rebuilt after its output was read, and the cause decomposition was added for the manuscript. E1 is exact for a design realized at its quadrature nodes and E2 is asymptotic, so no posterior was sampled and neither is an average over realized designs. The exact invariance of the summaries holds for known-variance Gaussian models; with estimated variances or random effects they would move with a departure and whether that movement could ever warn is untested. One target component, one covariate, one network geometry, a normal within-study covariate law on the logit arm, and departures acting on the mean only. The protocol went through thirteen rounds of critique; the manuscript has not been peer reviewed.
CMP-14.design: Exact computation on a four-component network, one scalar covariate, twelve arms in every state. The target interaction is identified by its own IPD trial, by a combination arm under additivity, by the between-study contrast in aggregate covariate means, by differing covariate variances (logit only), or not at all. E1: identity link, known variance, 504 scenarios crossing state, covariate spread, network size, interaction prior SD, discordance and synergy. E2: logit link, asymptotic, 72 scenarios.
CMP-14.n_sim: Exact and asymptotic computation: 504 E1 scenarios and 72 E2 scenarios, no Monte Carlo replicates
CMP-14.estimand: The within-trial interaction of the target component, true value 0.4; coverage of its nominal 95% interval
methods_compared: target-level likelihood to prior precision ratio

CMP-20.title: The exposure-rate covariance the Poisson aggregate likelihood assumes away
CMP-20.question: The aggregate Poisson likelihood multiplies an arm's total exposure by its mean modeled rate, which is exact only when exposure and rate are uncorrelated. The error is the factor 1 + rho CV(T) CV(lambda) per arm. How much bias does that put on a transported rate ratio at plausible levels of differential follow-up, and do exposure-weighted covariate summaries remove it?
CMP-20.design: A minimal anchored network, individual data on A versus C and arm totals on B versus C, with lognormal exposure solved so each arm's exposure-rate correlation and dispersions take registered values exactly. 234 attainable cells crossing the control-arm correlation, its difference in the treated arm, CV of exposure, CV of the rate and arm size; unweighted, exposure-weighted and borrowed-slope integration and a sensitivity bound. 1000 replicates per cell.

CMU-02.title: Do prior-sensitivity diagnostics catch the analyses that are actually wrong?
CMU-02.question: In a population-adjusted network a proper prior yields a proper posterior even where the likelihood identifies nothing, so a narrow interval can reflect the prior rather than the evidence. The diagnostics that would expose this exist. What are their operating characteristics: do they flag the analyses whose intervals actually miss the truth, and how often do they cry wolf?
CMU-02.answer: At the thresholds the literature suggests, they miss most of it. Pairing each warning with whether that replicate's own interval missed, a composite of four diagnostics has sensitivity 0.37 at a false-alarm rate of 0.16, falling to 0.13 outside two engineered geometries; the one sensitive rule fires on half the sound analyses too. Used as continuous scores the same statistics reach AUC 0.51 to 0.78, so this is a failure of thresholds rather than of the statistics. What no threshold repairs is that these diagnostics measure the prior's influence while the harm comes from the prior's location: with disconnected evidence and a tight prior four standard deviations from the truth, going from 100 to 400 per arm drops the warning rate from 0.98 to 0.01 while coverage stays near zero.
findings: Prespecified verdict: diagnostics fail at the thresholds the literature suggests. Composite sensitivity 0.366 (MCSE 0.002), false alarm 0.158; 0.127 and 0.025 outside the engineered positive controls.

Sensitivity and specificity trade off completely. Tight-and-loose prior refitting catches 0.83 of misses outside the controls and fires on 53% of covered replicates. Contraction, the prior-only benchmark and power-scaling keep false alarms low and catch almost nothing.

The composite adds almost nothing over its best component: 0.366 against contraction's 0.363, at a higher false-alarm rate. Requiring two of four rules to agree neither buys specificity nor recovers sensitivity.

More data makes the warning quieter while the answer stays wrong. Disconnected evidence, tight prior, true interaction four prior SDs away: coverage near zero at both sample sizes, warning rate 0.98 at 100 per arm and 0.01 at 400. Contraction is what every diagnostic reads as reassurance.

A first implementation measured power-scaling by posterior mean shift and found sensitivity 0.000 everywhere. That was our error: with a zero-centred prior, scaling the prior up and the likelihood down give identical posterior means, so the standard rule can never fire. Measured distributionally it works, and the verdict does not depend on the amendment.
The structural rank screen is the only rule with no false alarms at all, and it is blind to every failure where the contrast is estimable and the answer is still wrong.
CMU-02.not_answered: The other half of CMU-02, wiring these diagnostics into released software, is untouched; neither multinma nor cpaic is run. The model is conjugate Gaussian with an identity link, a correctly specified linear mean and known variances, so nothing transfers directly to a non-conjugate posterior where MCMC error enters and the diagnostics behave differently. Only automated thresholds are evaluated; a plot read by an experienced analyst is a different instrument. Thresholds were taken from the source literature and not tuned. CMP-14 is touched only for the generic aggregate-only interaction, not for component models, and IDN-06 is not addressed at all because this design contains no within-versus-between discrepancy.
CMU-02.design: A conjugate Gaussian population-adjusted network in which every piece of evidence reduces without loss to a normal observation, so the posterior and every power-scaled posterior are exact and no diagnostic is contaminated by MCMC noise. 120 scenarios crossing the evidence available about the weakly identified treatment, arm size, whether the truth agrees with the zero-centered prior, prior scale, and the target population. 2000 replicates each.
CMU-02.n_sim: 2000 per scenario, 240,000 datasets and 480,000 contrast evaluations
CMU-02.estimand: Target-population marginal C versus B mean difference, and the conditional interaction coefficient

COV-03.title: What an anchored comparison must balance on a non-collapsible scale
COV-03.question: On the log odds ratio scale a purely prognostic covariate changes the marginal effect. Does an anchored MAIC that balances only covariate means, as practice does, leave material bias, and does balancing the variance of the prognostic index remove it at acceptable cost in effective sample size?
COV-03.design: Anchored and unanchored binary-outcome comparisons, 108 cells crossing prognostic strength, the source-to-target ratio of prognostic index variance, target mean shift and effect modification; five methods including MAIC on means, on means and variances, on the prognostic index variance, and G-computation. 1000 replicates per cell.

COV-09.title: The same covariate name, two instruments
COV-09.question: When the source and target measure a matched effect modifier with different instruments, how is the MAIC estimate biased, does a reliability correction recover it, and can a bounded analysis over declared instrument differences contain the truth?
COV-09.answer: MAIC's bias from a modifier measured by different instruments follows a closed form in the instruments' offsets, slopes and the source reliability. A reliability correction removes it only when both trials use the same instrument; with differing instruments it left bias up to 0.18 and could undo a chance cancellation. An envelope of corrected intervals over declared instrument differences covered the truth at 1.4 to 2.9 times the naive width.
findings: Naive bias on its closed form: slope 0.992 (SE 0.009) over 45 scenarios; zero without modification.
Shared instrument: reliability-corrected bias within 3 MCSE in 12 of 12 scenarios with modification.

Differing instruments: corrected bias above 0.05 in 15 of 18 scenarios, up to 0.176; at reliability 0.6 a target offset cancelled the attenuation in the naive analysis (bias -0.018) and the correction removed the cancellation (0.172).
Bounded analysis over declared instrument differences: coverage 0.967 to 1.000, width 1.36 to 2.93 times naive.
COV-09.not_answered: Linear instruments and identity link only; misclassification of binary covariates and bridging-sample correction not run; target sampling error absent. Peer review has not been done.
COV-09.design: Continuous-outcome MAIC with a latent modifier recorded by the source and reported by the target through linear instruments with offsets, slopes and error; 45 cells crossing instrument pairs, source reliability and modification strength; naive, reliability-corrected and bounded analyses. 1000 replicates per cell.
COV-09.estimand: Target-population mean difference, A versus C
methods_compared: bounded analysis over declared instrument differences

COV-12.title: Reconstructing a target covariate from a median: when the mean is enough and when it is not
COV-12.question: When a target publication reports a skewed covariate as a median with IQR or range, how much error does reconstructing its marginal put into a target-standardized contrast, and is that error a function of the reconstructed mean alone?
COV-12.answer: Under an identity link with linear effect modification, yes: the contrast error is exactly the modification coefficient times the mean error. Under a logit link, no: the mean explains only 60% of the error's variance, because the reconstruction's spread and shape also enter. With strong skew and a reported range, a normal reconstruction biased the contrast by more than 1 on the identity scale and 0.4 on the log odds ratio scale, growing with sample size; a lognormal matched to the reported quantiles kept bias below 0.1.
findings: Registered test, contrast error net of the sample floor regressed on the modification coefficient times mean error: identity link slope 1.000, R^2 1.000; logit link slope 0.246, R^2 0.597.
Normal reconstruction (Wan et al.) with strong skew and a range: bias 1.15 (identity) and 0.42 (logit) at 200 patients; 2.15 (identity) at 1000, since the range grows with n.
Quantile-matched shifted lognormal: largest bias 0.092 across all 72 scenarios.
Without skew the lognormal matcher is not free: sampling asymmetry in the reported quantiles triggers it, and its bias reached 0.08, against 0.005 for the normal reconstruction.
COV-12.not_answered: One covariate with a known conditional model; estimated outcome models and multivariate marginals with dependence (CMP-15) are not covered. The lognormal matcher suits right skew only. ML-NMR integration is represented by direct integration. Two cells were run before a regressor correction and discarded unread. Peer review has not been done.
COV-12.design: A known conditional model integrated over target marginals reconstructed from a sample median with IQR or range; 72 scenarios crossing link, skewness, reported summary, target size (50 to 1000) and modification strength.
COV-12.estimand: Target-population marginal treatment effect (difference or log odds ratio)
methods_compared: integration over the target's own sample (floor)

COV-14.title: Covariate sets that differ across comparators, and the ranking read from them
COV-14.question: When one individual-data trial is compared with several aggregate comparators that report different covariates, does adjusting each contrast for everything it reports give a worse ranking than adjusting all contrasts for the common set, even though each contrast is less biased?
COV-14.answer: Neither adjustment rule protects the ranking. The common (intersection) set ranked better in 15 of 36 scenarios and the maximal sets in 19; which wins depends on whether the omission bias pushes a lower-ranked comparator past a higher one, which the data do not show. The registered inversion was not confirmed in the primary scenarios, whose pattern turned out to widen the top comparator's lead, but held in all six Fawsitt-like scenarios with similar populations. The intersection's per-contrast bias was a median 2.4 times the maximal. A bounded analysis over the other comparators' reported means covered at least 0.93 with similar comparator populations at little extra width.
findings: Registered primary (strongest covariate missing for the top comparator, similar populations, tied effects): maximal sets lower on both bias and wrong-top-rank probability in 3 of 3 scenarios; verdict MAXIMAL VINDICATED.
Fawsitt-like pattern, similar populations: intersection lower wrong-top-rank probability in 6 of 6 scenarios, up to 0.94 against 0.31.
The difference between the two analyses did not predict a wrong top rank (AUROC 0.567).
Bounded interval coverage at least 0.929 with similar comparator populations at 1.00 to 1.99 times the maximal width; 0.678 at worst with dispersed populations. Maximal-set coverage fell to 0.086.
COV-14.not_answered: Continuous outcome and independent covariates; non-collapsible outcomes, correlated omissions, a single ML-NMR network fit and overlap as a factor were not run. Three reporting patterns sample but do not exhaust where omissions can fall. Peer review has not been done.
COV-14.design: Unanchored MAIC of one trial against four comparators with nine covariates, 36 cells crossing reporting pattern, prognostic strength, similarity of comparator populations and separation of true effects, plus 8 control cells; maximal, intersection and bounded analyses. 1000 replicates per cell.
COV-14.estimand: B_k versus A mean difference in each comparator's population, and the ranking of the four
methods_compared: bounded interval over other comparators' reported means

DIA-02.title: The reported weight panel cannot see where support is missing
DIA-02.question: Every member of the overlap panel MAIC reports (Kish ESS, ESS percentage, entropy efficiency, maximum weight, top-share) is a symmetric function of the weights, so none can depend on where in covariate space the source fails to cover the target. Does that blindness matter in an ordinary covariate law, or do weight concentration and support geometry move together tightly enough that the panel is an adequate proxy?
DIA-02.answer: It matters. Two source populations that remove the same mass at the same threshold, one in the effect-modifying coordinate and one in a prognostic coordinate, give panels that agree to within 1.6% while one estimate is biased by 0.016 on the marginal risk difference and the other by less than 0.0001, and material error is 24 times as frequent in the first. Across the two placements every panel member sits within 0.005 of chance; region-specific ESS separates them almost perfectly and sliced optimal transport cost at 0.73, but a convex hull distance maximized over coordinates is as blind as the panel. The registered within-arm primary outcome reads the other way (panel 0.574, best geometric 0.592, rule returns refuted) because within one arm the hole placement is fixed and the outcome measures sampling noise, not geometry. Both readings are reported. Balance on the omitted moment, the comparator most likely to overturn the headline, was never fairly tested.
findings: The manipulation works in a plain multivariate normal law. With strong effect modification, a hole in the modifying coordinate biases MAIC's marginal risk difference by 0.0164 and a same-sized hole in a prognostic coordinate by -0.0001, while every panel member agrees between the two arms to within 1.6%. The refuting sentence, that such a counterexample needs configurations that do not occur, fails.

Across the two hole placements, over 16,000 replicates, the best panel member separates them at 0.505 against 0.5 for chance, standard error 0.004. Region-specific ESS separates them at 1.000 and sliced optimal transport cost at 0.726. Convex hull distance, though it reads position, separates at 0.503 because it is a maximum over coordinates and both arms remove an identical wedge.

The registered primary, AUROC against material error within the high-modification arm, returns refuted: best panel member 0.574, best geometric 0.592, a gap of 0.018 against a registered materiality of 0.10. Within one arm every replicate shares the hole placement, so the registered outcome asks which replicate drew a bad sample, and a concentration measure answers that as well as anything. The registered outcome was the wrong measurement for the proposition; it is reported as registered, not relabeled.

Two of three controls failed on parts of the grid. At eight covariates and moderate overlap MAIC's own error exceeds the 0.03 material threshold in 0.289 of replicates with no hole at all, the same threshold-below-noise defect IDN-05 documented. Leaving the modifier's second moment unmatched breaks the symmetry the manipulation rests on and the panels diverge by up to 91%. The analysis runs on the 12 of 48 cells the controls leave, all at good overlap.

Two of the three ESS definitions implemented are the same statistic when weights are normalized, so the measured comparability spread is Kish against entropy ESS: median 1.55 times, 90th percentile 3.50, maximum 15.5 on identical data.

DIA-03.title: Effective sample size tracks the error an analysis got by chance better than the error it got from adjusting on the wrong covariates
DIA-03.question: Every population adjustment arrives with a panel of numbers beside it: effective sample size, the same figure as a percentage, the largest weight, standardized differences before and after adjustment, a distance between populations. A committee reads them as evidence about whether to believe the estimate, and a widely quoted rule says to worry below an effective sample size of about 30 to 35. Scored as classifiers of realized error, with discrimination and calibration, against known truth and under a declared distribution of analyses, what are they worth?
DIA-03.answer: At the level at which a diagnostic is actually read, one analysis at a time, effective sample size tracks the error a study got by chance far better than the error it got from adjusting on the wrong covariates: AUROC 0.847 against the outcome-noise component and 0.813 against chance covariate imbalance between the source arms, both of which are functions of the covariates, the assignment and the weights, against 0.653 for the transport component that adjustment exists to remove. At the quoted cutoff of 35 it catches between a quarter and a third of material errors in every misspecification stratum, 0.309 where an effect modifier is omitted and the omission is diagnosable in principle, at specificity 0.926. No evaluated fixed cutoff met the registered requirement of sensitivity 0.80 at specificity 0.50 in every stratum. Three of the panel's members are provably one statistic, since ESS/n = 1/(1+CV^2(w)) exactly and area under the ROC curve is invariant to monotone transformation; a fourth, the post-weighting balance on matched moments, is zero at the solution of the calibration equations and among converged analyses cannot discriminate anything. On a decision-curve basis every rule in the panel is beaten by scrutinizing every analysis, up to an action threshold of 0.3.
findings: Prespecified verdict: the panel does not classify realized error at the thresholds in use. No rule reached sensitivity 0.80 with specificity 0.50 in every misspecification stratum. ESS below 35 reaches sensitivity 0.251 to 0.326 across strata at specificity 0.909 to 0.926.

The mechanism, registered before the run and holding at the level of a single analysis: effective sample size discriminates the outcome-noise component at AUROC 0.847 and the transport component at 0.653, a gap of 0.194, and the arm-imbalance component at 0.813. The two it reads well are the two that are functions of the covariates, the assignment and the weights, which is what the panel is built from.

Peer review changed this claim and the paper's title. Scored against SYSTEMATIC transport bias with the design cell as the unit, rather than against the realized transport component of one replicate, effective sample size reaches 0.808 rather than 0.653. That analysis does not rescue the panel either: the statistic that is identically zero reaches 0.708 on it, because 128 cells is a small sample in which the bias and every diagnostic move along the same overlap axis. Both levels are reported and the title now claims only the replicate-level result.

The panel is smaller than it looks, by algebra rather than by simulation. ESS, ESS as a percentage and the coefficient of variation of the weights had identical areas under the ROC curve to 0.0e+00 within a fixed source size. The matched-moment balance statistic never exceeded 1.4e-14 and its apparent AUROC of 0.550 is discrimination of floating-point residual, not of balance.

Silence is where the damage is. Across the 88 cells the ESS rule never fires in, the material-error rate runs from 0.045 to 0.835. The registered version of this claim, a spread across the cells it does fire in, was not met (0.150 against a prespecified 0.30) because those cells are all bad. A first draft called the silent-cell span a stronger version of the registered claim; peer review established that both spans are variation in predictive value, which moves with prevalence and case mix, so neither is a test of whether a threshold transports. That promotion is withdrawn and the leave-one-factor-level-out calibration is the evidence on transportability.

Decision-curve analysis: at action thresholds up to 0.3, flagging every analysis beats every rule in the panel. From 0.4 upwards three distinct statistics beat both alternatives, relative effective sample size, pre-weighting imbalance and Mahalanobis distance; the absolute cutoff that gets quoted is not among them at any threshold examined.

The same statistics work when they measure the actual gap. Pre-weighting imbalance predicts the unadjusted comparison's transport error at AUROC 0.891, against 0.655 for the same statistic applied to MAIC. These diagnostics are informative about the problem and uninformative about the solution: weighting sets to zero the very quantity they measure.

Our proposal, converting residual imbalance on a measured but unadjusted covariate into the units of the estimand with the source-estimated interaction, reaches 0.937 against the transport component over the diagnosable set where effective sample size as a percentage reaches 0.851. That gain of 0.086 misses the 0.10 we registered and is reported as a miss. Inside the omitted-modifier stratum alone the plain balance check on unmatched covariates beats it, 0.946 against 0.938, because there the covariate is always a modifier and converting imbalance into effect units only adds estimation noise. The conversion earns its keep exactly when the analyst does not know whether the unmatched covariate matters.

An adversarial critique of the design before the run found two arithmetic errors in the protocol: the dispersion factor was not the pure variance instrument it was described as wherever the cross-moment channel was on, and the target trial's variance was understated by a factor of two to three. Both were confirmed numerically and corrected before any result was seen.

Round one of review found the load-bearing claim of the paper wrong, and all three reviewers found it independently. The arm-imbalance component uses no outcome at all, and the noise component's variance is exactly sigma^2 (1/ESS_A + 1/ESS_C), so a weight statistic is its natural summary rather than merely correlated with it. Round one also found that the calibration split was perfectly confounded with the dispersion factor, because cells are enumerated with that factor varying fastest; leave-one-factor-level-out replaced it and the previous claim that overlap statistics calibrate worse than weight statistics was withdrawn as an artifact.
DIA-03.not_answered: The second half of DIA-03 is untouched: no PSIS-LOO is computed at any hierarchical level and grouped study-level leave-one-out is no more implemented here than in the packages, so the mismatch between the level at which cross-validation is reported and the level at which the prediction is made remains open. DIA-06 is answered only in part; two estimator families and no adjustment are compared on identical replicates, but ML-NMR, NMI, doubly robust estimators and flexible learners are absent. The outcome is continuous with an identity link, which is what buys the exact error decomposition and is also the largest restriction: nothing here transfers to non-collapsible effect measures or time-to-event outcomes, where part of the error is a collapsibility artifact rather than an adjustment failure. Covariates are normal, comparisons are anchored, conditional constancy holds, and target moments are exact. The deployment weights are a declared judgment and nothing in this program measured them, which is why the primary results are within strata.
DIA-03.design: An anchored indirect comparison with a continuous outcome and an identity link, chosen so that the realized error of a linear estimator splits exactly into arm imbalance, transport error and outcome noise, so each diagnostic can be scored against each component separately: two of the three are functions of the covariates, the assignment and the weights, which is what the panel is built from, and the third is what adjustment exists to remove. 128 cells crossing an omitted effect modifier, a cross-moment modifier that no baseline table could reveal, overlap, source size, how correlated the omitted modifier is with the adjustment set, and a target dispersion ratio that destroys effective sample size while adding no bias where the modifier structure is correct. 4000 replicates per cell, four estimators. Primary results are reported within misspecification strata rather than over a mixture, so no investigator-chosen frequency enters the headline.
DIA-03.estimand: Transported A versus C mean difference in the target superpopulation; the anchored A versus B contrast as a secondary reference
methods_compared: MAIC matching means and standard deviations

DIA-14.title: A quantitative bias analysis verdict scored as a classifier
DIA-14.question: How often does a QBA declare a MAIC decision robust when the true bias would reverse it, how does that depend on the elicited region rather than the method, and does oracle recovery reveal it?
DIA-14.design: Unanchored MAIC with an unmeasured binary confounder; elicited bias regions with exclusion probability set directly, three error directions and three widths; grid and probabilistic QBA scored on false reassurance and false fragility; 18 cells, 2000 replicates each.

EST-06.title: When two sponsors' MAICs disagree: how often, why, and which common target resolves it
EST-06.question: When two sponsors run MAIC on the same two trials, each weighting its own data to the other trial, how often do their conclusions reverse, how much of that is a real difference in target population rather than sampling error or differing adjustment sets, and which common-target remedy recovers the decision population's effect?
EST-06.answer: Reversal is mostly a real target difference and it is common: with the modifier's zero-effect point between the two populations, sponsors disagreed in sign in 23% to 56% of analyses at separations up to 1 SD and modification up to 0.4, and moving the point outside the populations cut that by a median 0.31. The two sponsors' estimates are correlated, which a reversal calculation must use. Under linear modification the plain average of the two analyses is as accurate for the midpoint population as transporting both trials there.
findings: Between-minus-outside reversal probability exceeded 0.20 in 11 of 18 common-set configurations (median 0.31); the refuting sentence, that reversals need extreme configurations, fails.
Correlation between the two sponsors' estimates 0.14 to 0.99; a bivariate normal with that correlation predicted the reversal probability within 0.036, and ignoring it erred by up to 0.44.
A sponsor that left the modifier out of its weights was biased by 0.10 to 0.91 against its own target.
Transport of both trials to a declared population and the average of the two analyses: largest bias 0.024 and 0.027, median RMSE 0.231 and 0.239.
EST-06.not_answered: Linear modification and a continuous outcome; with nonlinear modification or a non-collapsible scale the average is not the midpoint effect. The arbitrated indirect comparison and measurement differences between trials were not run. Peer review has not been done.
EST-06.design: Two trials with linear modification of one treatment, analyzed by two sponsors each weighting its own trial to the other's population; 108 scenarios crossing separation, modification strength, the position of the zero-effect point, trial sizes and adjustment sets, plus controls; transport of both trials to a declared population and the average of the two analyses as remedies.
EST-06.estimand: B-versus-A mean difference in each sponsor's target population and in a declared decision population
methods_compared: transport of both trials to a declared population

IDN-05.title: A violation twice the size that would change a decision raises the shared effect modifier check's alarm rate from 1.3% to 4.5%
IDN-05.question: Population adjustment across a network assumes that a covariate modifies the effect of every active treatment in a class in the same way. There is one published within-network check on that assumption: fit the model with a single interaction shared across the class, refit with treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time, and compare the posteriors and the model fit. Its authors say it likely has low power. Nobody has measured it, there is no threshold that separates a pass from a failure, and there is no statement of what a pass licenses. Scored against a known truth under a declared distribution of networks, what is it worth?
IDN-05.answer: The check does not have the resolution to test the assumption it is read as testing. Against a violation already twice the size that would change a decision, the DIC rule fires in 0.045 [0.029, 0.070] of analyses, against 0.013 [0.005, 0.029] when the assumption holds exactly: a violation that doubles the error that matters moves the alarm rate by about three percentage points. The result does not depend on where the cut is put. Scored threshold-free, the DIC difference ranks a violated network above an intact one with an AUROC of 0.557 [0.517, 0.596] at that violation, so no threshold recovers a ranking the statistic does not contain. The posterior standard deviation of the interaction contrast runs 0.30 to 1.64 against the 0.153 that would make a transported estimate materially wrong, which is why. The equivalence reading, the only one that could confirm rather than merely fail to contradict, fired zero times in 3,200 opportunities, including every replicate where the assumption held exactly; that is a statement about precision, and partly about the prior, since independent normal(0, 2.5) priors already place 0.965 of the contrast beyond the margin. Following the check is still better than not: relaxing exactly what it fires on beats relaxing everything at every target displacement and beats imposing the restriction at every displacement except zero, where the two are indistinguishable.
findings: Detection barely moves with the violation. Pooled over all eight design strata, 400 replicates each, the DIC cut at 5 fires in 0.013 [0.005, 0.029] under the global null, 0.045 [0.029, 0.070] at a contrast of 0.30 that leaves the transported estimate wrong by twice the material threshold, 0.147 at 0.60 and 0.453 at 1.20, which is eight times the decision boundary and a stress test rather than a plausible violation.

The finding survives without any threshold. Scored as a classifier, the DIC difference separates a violated network from an intact one with an AUROC of 0.557 [0.517, 0.596] at a contrast of 0.30, 0.681 [0.644, 0.718] at 0.60 and 0.843 [0.815, 0.870] at 1.20; against material error itself it reaches 0.666 at a target one standard deviation away. This analysis was prespecified, computed from the first run onward, and omitted from the first two drafts until three reviewers asked for it.

The reason is resolution. The posterior standard deviation of the difference between the two treatments' effect modifiers runs 0.30 to 1.64 on the log-odds scale across strata, against 0.153 for the difference that makes the transported estimate materially wrong. An earlier draft led with a prior-removed version of this quantity; its own sensitivity arm showed the quantity is unstable, so the measured posterior standard deviation is what is reported.

The procedure cannot give an all-clear. The equivalence reading, P(|difference| <= 0.153) > 0.95, fired in 0 of 3,200 covariate-checks, including every replicate where the two modifiers were identical by construction. This is a precision result: firing needs a posterior standard deviation below about 0.078 and the tightest stratum reaches 0.30. It is also prior-dependent in the other direction, since independent normal(0, 2.5) priors on the two coefficients put 0.965 of their contrast beyond the margin before any data are seen, above the 0.95 threshold at which the complementary margin rule fires.

The registered verdict fails, and a perfect check would have failed it too. The upper 95% bound on the probability that a passed analysis is materially wrong is 0.697, deployment- weighted, against a registered 0.10. But an oracle that knows the true interaction specification is materially wrong 0.639 of the time on the same replicates, so the check's excess over that oracle is 0.036 and is negative at small target displacements. With a threshold of 0.03 absolute risk, the estimation error of a six-study network alone exceeds it in about half of analyses when the assumption holds exactly. A threshold on total error charges a diagnostic for noise it was never built to detect.

The check is blind to what determines the harm. Its output reads only the fitted network, so its pass rate is identical at every target displacement to the last digit. Over the same fits the probability that a passed analysis is materially wrong rises from 0.427 to 0.723, an excess over the noise floor of 0.296 against a registered 0.20. The first half of that is an algebraic identity that verifies the bookkeeping; the second is empirical.

The three readings are not three procedures. The DIC rule fires without the interval rule in 0.0006 of covariate-checks and the interval rule fires without DIC in 0.106, so the DIC cut is very nearly a strict subset of the interval rule rather than a second opinion. Under the global null they differ in type I error by 0.080 on the drifting covariate and 0.087 pooling both. The 95% interval rule runs at about twice its nominal rate, 0.075 [0.046, 0.120] with no treatment-effect heterogeneity and 0.110 [0.074, 0.161] with it, so avoiding covariate selection does not deliver nominal coverage.
A fire is not a diagnosis. When a violation is present the interval rule fires on the covariate that is shared exactly in up to 0.388 of replicates.

Following the check beats the alternatives, but not uniformly, and the ranking of the alternatives is the surprise. Deployment-weighted and paired on the same replicates, relaxing exactly what fired beats relaxing everything at every displacement on both absolute and squared error, and beats imposing the restriction at displacements 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 but is indistinguishable from it at 0 (-0.00005, 95% CI [-0.00069, 0.00059]), where there is nothing to transport. Relaxing everything is worse than imposing the restriction, because the relaxed model spends precision the network does not have; it also fails its sampler diagnostics in 0.068 of replicates and 0.24 in the worst cell. The worst diagnostic reached by any model is R-hat 5.13 with effective sample size 1.03, in a singly-relaxed fit.

Knowing the target is worth more than knowing the check statistic. Held out across design factors, the check statistic alone discriminates material error at an AUROC of 0.48 to 0.63, close to chance; adding the target displacement raises it to 0.69 to 0.83. A one-term mapping from the statistic to the probability of material error transports across network size, covariate spread and heterogeneity with absolute errors of 0.013 to 0.058, and fails across drift with an error of 0.469.

On a decision-curve basis, distrusting every adjusted analysis has higher net benefit than every rule in the panel at every action threshold from 0.05 to 0.60. This restates the noise floor rather than measuring the check: with material error present in 0.675 of passing analyses, most of it sampling noise no covariate check can predict, treat-all dominates almost regardless of what the check does.

Two software findings, against multinma 0.9.1.9002 (commit 8489bd83). The package documents class_interactions = 'exchangeable' and raises 'not yet supported', so the hierarchical relaxation this catalog entry proposed as the way forward cannot be fitted; the entry's claim that it ships in the package is wrong for this version. And under the default class_interactions = 'common', an x:.trt term in a regression formula is silently demoted to the class level, so an analyst who follows the published recipe by editing the formula alone fits the shared model twice and can never find evidence against sharing.

Two adversarial critiques before the run found nine issues between them that changed the design, and each found something the other missed. Peer review then found more, including two errors in this study's own code: contraction was divided by the standard deviation of a prior the prior-sensitivity arm was not fitted under, which inverted the reported direction of that arm's result, and the primary bound was a Wilson interval on the unweighted risk printed beside a deployment-weighted point estimate. Both were derived by reviewers from the published numbers alone, without access to the code.
IDN-05.not_answered: The design is a best case in several specific ways that favour the check, and failures attributable to those idealizations are conservative; no general lower-bound claim is made, because three features cut the other way. The true marginal reference risk in the target is supplied to the estimator. Covariates are normal with known target moments and study covariate means are drawn independently of study baselines and of the random treatment effects, so the ecological route identifying the aggregate-only treatment's interaction is unbiased by construction. Conditional constancy holds and only one covariate drifts, linearly. Against that: the fits are fixed-effect while half the cells generate random treatment effects, which is a second specification error that inflates firing; the likelihood is integrated over 64 quadrature points and refitting at 256 changes the DIC verdict in 8.3% of a 24-network subset, which is noise belonging to the implementation and not to the evidence, and 256 points is not demonstrated to be converged; and a single individual-level study is an assumption about the network rather than necessarily a pessimistic one. Beyond that: what a second individual-level study would buy is not measured, that factor having been dropped to pay for treatment-effect heterogeneity. With two active treatments and two covariates, multiplicity across covariates and the selection involved in reading the widest of several pairwise differences are not measured. Where treatment-effect heterogeneity is present the estimand is not cleanly defined, since truth is set at a random effect of zero while a fixed-effect model targets a function of the realized studies; primary results are repeated on the sixteen homogeneous cells and do not change. The hierarchical middle ground between shared and independent interactions could not be fitted because the package does not implement it, and we did not implement it ourselves: that is a reason for its absence, not a justification. The five decision rules scored here are our formalizations of an exploratory published practice, not published rules, and their operating characteristics are ours. Fifty replicates per cell gives a per-cell standard error of 0.065, so nothing is read off a single cell.
IDN-05.design: A multilevel network meta-regression with a binomial outcome and a logit link, one individual-level study and the rest aggregate, two active treatments in one class of which only one has individual data. Drift is carried by one covariate and parameterized as the contrast between the two treatments' interactions; a second covariate is shared exactly and supplies a type I error observation from the same fits. 32 cells crossing drift, network size, between-study covariate spread and treatment-effect heterogeneity, 50 replicates each, four fits per replicate forming the complete model lattice, plus eight amendment cells at the decision boundary, a prior-sensitivity arm and an integration-sensitivity check. The target population is not a design factor because the check reads only the fitted network and cannot depend on it; one set of fits is scored at four target displacements, and the reference intercept is solved separately for each so displacement moves the treatment contrast and not the baseline risk.
IDN-05.n_sim: 50 per cell, 2,000 networks and 8,960 ML-NMR fits: 6,400 over the 32 registered cells, 1,600 in the amendment arm, 960 in the prior-sensitivity arm. That last arm ran at 30 replicates per cell against the 100 registered, a departure found in round-two review and disclosed in the protocol.
IDN-05.estimand: Marginal risk difference for the aggregate-only treatment versus the individual-data treatment in a target population, with the population-average conditional log-odds effect as the mechanism scale
methods_compared: check first, then relax exactly what fired

IDN-10.title: A transported control-arm check carries no information about the anchored contrast
IDN-10.question: Does agreement between a MAIC-transported control arm and the target's observed control arm tell an analyst whether the anchored relative effect is biased?
IDN-10.answer: No. The check tests prognostic transport, which an anchored contrast does not need, and cannot see effect-modification transport, which it does. A prognostic shift raised the alarm rate to 0.48 while the contrast was nearly unbiased (bias -0.03 to -0.06); a modifier shift biased the log odds ratio by 0.30 with the alarm rate at 0.044. Pooled over 18,000 analyses the check's AUROC for a biased contrast was 0.50.
findings: Prognostic shift of 0.6 SD, no modifier shift: alarm rate 0.41 to 0.48, contrast bias -0.03 to -0.06.
Modifier shift of 0.6 SD, no prognostic shift: alarm rate 0.044 to 0.050, contrast bias 0.28 to 0.30, coverage 0.78 to 0.82.
At every threshold on |z| the detection rate equaled the false-alarm rate (0.21 against 0.21 at 1.96); AUROC 0.502.
The check targets the right assumption only in unanchored comparisons, where the relative effect depends on prognostic transport; that case was not simulated.
IDN-10.not_answered: Binary outcome only; survival-curve and RMST versions, unanchored comparisons, offsetting prognostic mechanisms and outcome-definition or follow-up differences are not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
IDN-10.design: Anchored binary-outcome MAIC, individual data on A versus C and arm counts on B versus C; an unmeasured prognostic covariate and an unmeasured modifier of A's effect shifted independently between populations; 18 scenarios crossing both shifts and target size.
IDN-10.estimand: Anchored B-versus-A marginal log odds ratio in the target; the check's alarm as a classifier of material bias
methods_compared: transported control-arm check at several thresholds

MIS-01.title: Missing covariate values in the individual-data trial of a MAIC
MIS-01.question: When a matched covariate is missing for some patients in the individual-data trial, when is complete-case MAIC biased, and do inverse-probability-of-observation weighting and multiple imputation repair it?
MIS-01.answer: Complete-case MAIC bias is set by the missingness mechanism, not the rate. It is unbiased when missingness depends only on matched covariates, including the missing covariate itself, and biased already at 15% missingness when it depends on an unmatched effect modifier, the outcome with modification, or an unmatched covariate in one arm only. Weighting and imputation repair the missing-at-random cases (imputation with arm interactions most reliably) but are biased by up to 0.22 when missingness depends on the missing covariate itself, where complete case is not.
findings: Complete case within 3 MCSE of zero in all 24 scenarios predicted unbiased and beyond 3 MCSE in all 4 predicted-biased scenarios at 15% missingness.
Missingness in one arm driven by an unmatched prognostic covariate: complete-case bias -0.34 at 15% and -0.65 at 30%, with no effect modification.
Missingness driven by the missing covariate: complete case within 0.035; observation weighting and imputation biased by up to 0.22.
Imputation without arm interactions carried small systematic bias (up to 0.05); observation weighting failed with extreme weights when 60% to 95% of one arm was missing.
MIS-01.not_answered: Missing outcomes, binary outcomes, STC, overlap levels and pattern-mixture sensitivity analysis not run; single-driver mechanisms only. Peer review has not been done.
MIS-01.design: Continuous-outcome MAIC with one partly missing matched covariate, one observed matched covariate and one unmatched covariate; 36 cells crossing missingness rate, six mechanisms and whether the unmatched covariate modifies the effect; complete case, observation weighting and congenial or generic imputation. 1000 replicates per cell.
MIS-01.estimand: Target-population mean difference, A versus C, in the anchored MAIC

MIS-03.title: What conditioning on sampled target moments costs
MIS-03.question: Population adjustment treats a target trial's published covariate means and standard deviations as exact, though they are sample estimates. By how much does that cost interval coverage at realistic sample sizes, and what would a publication have to report for a correction to work?
MIS-03.answer: Two things, established by different means. Analytically: the variance a standard interval omits is (1-2k)Var_T(tau)/n_T to first order, where k is how far the target trial's own treatment effect is modified by the same covariates as the source trial's, so the sign is set by a quantity the usual inputs do not identify; and a correction adding only the positive term is closer to the right variance than doing nothing only when k < 1/4. Empirically, and only in an exploratory subset: the omission runs from 9.5% too much variance to 14.9% too little and moves coverage between 92.1% and 96.2%. The registered analysis is uninformative and the confirmatory coverage question remains open.
findings: The prespecified analysis returned uninformative. Its gates require the reference interval and the negative controls to be nominal, and at poor overlap the Wald sandwich undercovers by up to 7 points for every method including scenarios with no effect modification at all, where the population omission is exactly zero. That is a source-variance failure, not a target-moment one.

The sign of the omission is an analytic identity, not a simulation finding: (1-2k)Var_T(tau)/n_T. Regressing the measured omission on it across all 216 scenarios with effect modification gives a slope of 1.003 (SE 0.042). An earlier draft claimed the simulation located the cancellation point; peer review corrected that and the claim was retracted.

The two corrections an analyst can deploy add only the positive term and omit the cross-covariance. They beat doing nothing only when k < 1/4, and are worse than doing nothing between 1/4 and 1/2. The design has no interior k with which to test this, so no recommendation is made for intermediate alignment. A draft claim that they help whenever k < 1/2 was wrong and was corrected in review.

In the exploratory subset the status quo was the only method to leave 93% to 97% coverage, and it left in both directions. Magnitude tracks the ratio of source to target information, so a large source trial matched to a small target publication is the worst case, not a small target trial.
Peer review left a standing recommendation of major revision. The confirmatory question needs a fresh registered run with an ex ante overlap restriction or a validated source variance estimator.
MIS-03.not_answered: The registered coverage question is not confirmatorily answered: every usable coverage result comes from a post-run restriction conditioning on an observed outcome. One estimator, one outcome type, one information structure. Covariates are multivariate normal, which is also the assumption the deployable correction is derived under, so it is measured under conditions favorable to it; skewed, bounded and categorical covariates are untested. The outcome is continuous and the effect additive, so marginal and conditional effects coincide, and nothing transfers directly to binary or time-to-event outcomes, where MAIC is most used. Effect modification lies exactly in the span of the matched moments, so this is a variance result under correct identification and says nothing about bias. The target moments and the target treatment effect come from the same trial, which is the common case but not the only one. STC, ML-NMR, ML-UMR and NMI have different sensitivities and are not covered. EST-07's other components, model uncertainty in reconstructed correlations, inclusion-criteria ambiguity and secular drift, are not sampling error and are untouched. The alignment parameter imposes exact non-negative proportionality between source and target modifier coefficients, so modifier sets differing in direction or overlapping only partially are untested.
MIS-03.design: Anchored MAIC on a continuous outcome, with the target trial's participants generated and then discarded so the estimator sees only a published baseline table. 252 scenarios crossing source size, target size, overlap, effect-modification strength calibrated to a fixed target-population standard deviation, the alignment between the two trials' effect modification, and whether the analyst's borrowed correlation is correct.
MIS-03.estimand: Target-superpopulation marginal A versus B mean difference, exact in closed form
